headline: High-risk shared filesystem and write-capable pair create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write the user filesystem, and agent_a explicitly shares state with other instances via filesystem. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge where agent_b can ingest agent_a outputs or shared files as trusted text. No direct evidence of a parser exploit is provided, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_b reads files produced by agent_a without provenance checks
IF both agents operate in the same writable workspace
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Require provenance tags on shared files
Disable automatic ingestion of peer-generated files
Review any shared-file prompts before execution

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a touches source code and files in cwd, while agent_b touches datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration files. Both have filesystem access, so sensitive material can cross between them through the shared workspace. The profiles do not show uncontrolled third-party upload by either agent, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in the shared cwd
IF either agent copies peer-visible files into its outputs
mitigations: Use separate directories with OS permissions
Mount only the minimum required files into each agent
Redact secrets before sharing artifacts
Audit outputs for accidental file inclusion

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, read and write the filesystem, and agent_a can modify git state. In a shared workspace, concurrent writes and git mutations can overwrite each other or corrupt state. Because agent_a explicitly supports shared filesystem state and no locking is stated, the default conflict risk is high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout
IF writes occur concurrently without external locking
mitigations: Assign one writer per repository
Serialize git operations with a lock
Use separate clones per agent
Disable concurrent shell writes in shared paths

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_a can generate code or file changes that agent_b may then consume, and both expose stdin/stdout plus filesystem channels. The profiles do not state that agent_b verifies agent_a's outputs before acting, but they also do not show autonomous downstream actions like email or deployment. That supports a medium cascading-error rating.
conditions: IF agent_b treats agent_a output as authoritative input
IF agent_a writes artifacts that agent_b later executes or summarizes
mitigations: Insert a human review step between agents
Require validation of generated files before use
Mark agent_a outputs as untrusted by default
Limit agent_b to read-only review of agent_a artifacts

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_b explicitly handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration files, while agent_a handles source code and files in cwd. The profiles show different data classes and different vendor/runtime contexts, but no residency or certification details. Because compliance mismatch is plausible yet undocumented, medium is the safest choice under uncertainty.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace
IF one agent's logging or retention policy differs from the other's
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace
Document retention and deletion rules for both agents
Route sensitive workloads only to the compliant agent
Review vendor/data-processing terms before deployment
